html:
"Plain-Pottery culture" is the map's label, from 500 BCE to 100 CE, for an Iron Age culture in the forests of the eastern Baltic region and the upper Dnieper. The label is not a standard English name, and which culture it means is not certain.

It most likely stands for the Dnieper-Dvina culture of the upper Dnieper and Western Dvina rivers, around today's Smolensk and Vitebsk, from about the 700s BCE to the 300s CE. Much of its later pottery was plain and smooth-walled, unlike the wares of its western neighbour, the Brushed Pottery culture, which may explain the label. Its people lived on small hillforts, raised cattle and pigs, farmed small plots, and hunted and fished. Iron came slowly into use.

Most scholars think these people spoke Baltic languages; river names of Baltic origin are found across the area. To the north lived the Finno-Ugric forest peoples, and to the south the Milograd culture. From the 500s CE Slavs moved into the region, and the Krivichs, an East Slavic tribe, came to hold the upper Dnieper and Dvina.
